deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler's fourth example of a pinned–pinned column of length a whose flexural rigidity ('moment de roideur') varies along the axis. Here the rigidity at height x is (α+βx/a)^2·Ekk, i.e. λ=1/2 in his general family. The buckling equation is Ekk(α+βx/a)^2 y'' + P y = 0. Substitute s = α+βx/a, so d²y/dx² = (β²/a²) d²y/ds². With nn = P a²/(β² Ekk) this becomes the homogeneous (Euler–Cauchy) equation s² y'' + nn y = 0.

The trial solution y = s^μ gives μ(μ−1)+nn = 0, so μ = 1/2 ± √(1/4−nn) and y = A s^{μ1} + B s^{μ2}.

Cases nn ≤ 1/4. If nn < 1/4 the exponents are real and distinct. A nontrivial combination cannot vanish at both ends s=α and s=α+β, because s^{μ1−μ2} is strictly monotone. So a load P = nnβ²Ekk/a² with nn<1/4 cannot bend the column. If nn = 1/4 the solution is y = (A + B ln s)√s, which again has at most one zero, so the same conclusion holds.

Case nn > 1/4. Put v = √(nn−1/4). Euler rewrites the imaginary powers s^{±iv} = cos(v ln s) ± i sin(v ln s), so y = b sin(ζ + v ln s)·√s.
- y(α)=0 gives ζ = −v ln α.
- The first nontrivial zero at s=α+β requires v ln(1+β/α) = π.
- Hence nn = 1/4 + π²/[ln(1+β/α)]², and the critical load is P = (1/4 + π²/[ln(1+β/α)]²)·β²·Ekk/a². Any smaller force produces no bending.

Checks:
- As β→0, β²(1/4 + π²α²/β²(1+O(β))) → π²α²Ekk/a², the Euler load of a uniform column of rigidity α²Ekk.
- On the next page, with α=1 and end-rigidity ratio m=1+β, this becomes P=(m−1)²(1/4+π²/(ln m)²)Ekk/a².
errors: Typographical: the printed formulas read 'l(+β/α)' for l(1+β/α) in both the expression for nn and for P (the line above correctly has l(1+β/α)).
Section numbering: the page goes from the continuation of §XXX (previous page) directly to §XXXII; no §XXXI appears. This is likely a misnumbering in the original print, not a mathematical error.
Minor gap: Euler takes the first zero (v ln(1+β/α)=π) as giving the smallest buckling load without remarking that the other zeros kπ give larger loads. This is the obvious and correct choice.
Minor gap: the non-vanishing argument for nn≤1/4 is asserted ('il est clair'), not proved. It is correct.

ideas.what: Reduction of the buckling equation for a column whose rigidity is the square of a linear function to an equidimensional ODE, solved by power functions s^μ
ideas.modern_name: Euler–Cauchy (equidimensional) equation; exact buckling load of a tapered column with EI ∝ (linear)^2
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (the equation bears his name); the tapered-column solution is usually attributed to Euler in the history of buckling, and it reappears in Dinnik and Timoshenko-type handbooks
ideas.where_published: E238 itself (Mém. Acad. Berlin 13, 1757/1759); Euler–Cauchy equations also treated in Euler's Institutiones calculi integralis; discussed by Truesdell, The Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies (Opera omnia II 11₂)

ideas.what: Converting imaginary exponents s^{±iv} into cos(v ln s), sin(v ln s), giving the oscillatory solution √s·sin(ζ+v ln s)
ideas.modern_name: Euler's formula applied to complex powers; complex characteristic roots of Euler–Cauchy equations

ideas.what: Threshold nn=1/4: no eigenfunction (no buckling) for nn≤1/4, oscillatory solutions only for nn>1/4
ideas.modern_name: Non-oscillation/oscillation threshold 1/4 for x²y''+cy=0 (prototype of Kneser's oscillation criterion; related to the Hardy-inequality constant)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Kneser (1893) for the general criterion; the Euler-equation case is classical folklore

ideas.what: Closed-form critical load P=(1/4+π²/ln²(1+β/α))β²Ekk/a² and its reduction to the cylindrical Euler load as β→0
ideas.modern_name: Critical buckling load of a non-prismatic (tapered) pinned–pinned column
ideas.where_published: E238; discussed by Truesdell 1960 and in the history of column theory (Timoshenko, History of Strength of Materials)

missed.claim: Euler's case split (no buckling for nn≤1/4, buckling only when nn>1/4) is exactly the oscillation threshold 1/4 that later underlies Kneser's oscillation theorem and the sharp Hardy constant. Euler states it as a physical statement about loads. This is a mild historical anticipation, but the Euler-equation case is so standard that specialists would not find it new.
missed.quote: si nn < 1/4 ... une force P = nnββ.Ekk/aa, n'est pas capable de faire plier la colonne. Il en est encore de même si nn = 1/4
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only as a historical note: the earliest appearance of the 1/4 oscillation threshold in a mechanical eigenvalue problem. No new mathematics follows.

deep.surprise_reason: Correct, routine solution of an Euler–Cauchy buckling equation, giving a known and credited closed-form tapered-column load. The E238 tapered-column examples are discussed in Truesdell's commentary. The 1/4 threshold is a minor anticipation of Kneser-type criteria but is folklore for this equation.
